title: Permissions in a booking product
metaTitle: Show a guest what they can book
excerpt: Show a guest what they can book, and why a time or service is unavailable. Hiding the control makes a booked-out day look broken. A reason makes it look honest.
alt: Curved library shelves packed with books, seen from a balcony, a collection where some shelves are clearly in reach and some are not.
caption: You can see the shelf. You should also see whether you may take the book. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Should booked-out times disappear?
faqs.answer: A day with missing hours looks broken on a phone, and a hurried guest will assume the calendar failed to load. Show times that are gone as unavailable, with a plain label such as Taken, and show bookable times as tappable. The contrast should be in the text, not only in a faded color.

faqs.question: What if the guest can see a service but cannot book it?
faqs.answer: Say why before they pick a time. Members only, this location only, or a required detail you still need are reasons. Put the reason where the button would be, and put the path to qualify if there is one. Letting them reach the last step and then failing is how a rule gets reported as a bug.

faqs.question: How should phone permission prompts be handled?
faqs.answer: Explain the request in your own screen before the system dialog. If they deny calendar or notification access, keep the booking working. Show the manual path that remains, such as adding the time themselves from the confirmation. A dead button after a denial feels like the booking broke.

markdown:
Booking product permissions UX is how a guest on a phone, in a hurry, learns what they can book and why a thing they expected is unavailable. Show the action. Say the reason. A hidden button feels like a bug, and they do not have time to debug your calendar.

They arrived to take a time. Every withheld time, service, or staff member is a small refusal. Refusals are fine. Silent refusals send them to the phone. The sentence you skipped becomes a conversation your front desk has to finish.

## What the guest can do, in the first view

They should be able to tell, without a help page, which services they can book, which times are open, and what is blocking them if something obvious is missing.

Open times look tappable. Taken times stay visible and say Taken. A staff member who is not bookable by the public does not appear in the public list. A service they can see and cannot book shows the reason in the slot where the times would have been.

Do not make availability a color lesson. Gray versus brand color fails in sunlight and fails for people who do not see that difference. The W3C's Web Content Accessibility Guidelines ask for content that is perceivable, operable, and understandable. [The WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is the short document to read before you ship a legend that says "light gray means unavailable." Write Taken. Write Open. Let color repeat the word, not replace it.

On a phone, the reason has to be in the first view of that service. A tooltip that appears on hover does not exist for a thumb. A reason behind an info icon is a second tap they may not make. Put the sentence in the layout.

## Hide, disable, or explain

Hide what this guest should never be offered. Another guest's booking details. Staff notes. A service you only sell by invoice. An internal hold. Showing those and disabling them teaches the guest that the product is full of doors that will not open.

Disable, and explain, what they know they might do and currently cannot. A time that is taken. A service that requires a membership they do not have. A reschedule that is outside the window. The control stays in the place their eye goes, it does not fire, and the sentence says what would change it.

Explain without a fake button when there is nothing to press. "This location is not taking online bookings. Call the desk." If you show a phone number, it should be tappable. The explanation is the design. A grayed-out Book now with no sentence is the version that generates screenshots in your support chat.

The accidental fourth state is a hole in the page. The times fail to render, the button is not in the markup, and the guest sees a heading and a blank. That is what a loading bug looks like. If the blank is actually a rule, you have disguised a rule as a defect. Say the rule.

## Rules a hurried guest will hit

Members only, or new clients only. Say it on the service before the calendar. If they can fix it in the product, give the path. Join, then book. If they cannot fix it here, say who can help, in one line. Do not collect their name and then reveal the rule.

Location and travel limits. A guest who can book the city studio and not the pop-up should see both named, with the closed one explained. Hiding the pop-up makes them think you forgot it. They will search for it. Search is the next article. Permissions should make that search unnecessary for the common case.

Lead time and cutoff. If they cannot book tomorrow because you require two days' notice, the calendar should say that on the closed days. "Booked" is the wrong word for "too soon." Use the real reason. Too soon, taken, and closed are different facts. Mixing them trains guests to distrust the word you chose.

Reschedule and cancel. After they have a booking, the confirmation is the place these actions live. If the window has passed, keep the action visible and say why it no longer works. "Changes close the day before" is a rule they can remember. A missing Change button makes them think the email link broke.

Who the booking is for. If a guest can book for someone else, the form should say whose name will be on the booking. If they cannot, and they try to, do not wait for a staff member to bounce it. A line on the form is enough: "Use the name of the person who will attend."

Staff accounts versus guest links. Review the public link in a private window. A staff session will show extra services and extra times, and you will approve a screen the guest never gets. The permission design is whatever the private window shows.

## Phone permissions are part of this screen

The operating system will ask for calendar, notifications, or location if you ask it to. Those dialogs are permissions too. They are easy to waste.

Ask in your interface first, in a sentence that says the benefit and the alternative. "Add this time to your calendar. You can also save the email and add it yourself." Then call the system dialog. If they deny it, the booking must still succeed. Show the confirmation with the time written out, and a control to add it manually. A denied prompt that leaves a spinner where the confirmation should be feels like the payment failed.

Do not ask for location before they have seen a time, unless the location chooses which times exist. If it does, say that. "We use your location to show the nearest studio." If they deny it, let them pick a studio from a list. A map that stays empty is a hidden list. Lists are operable. Mystery maps are not.

Notification permission can wait until the booking exists. Asking on the first screen, before a time is chosen, is a tax on a hurried guest. After the confirmation, "Remind me" is a motive they understand.

## Write the reason before the last step

The costly pattern is a full form followed by "You are not allowed to book this." They spent the hurry on fields you could have blocked at the top. Move the check earlier. If the block depends on a detail they must type, such as a membership number, ask for that detail first, check it, then show times.

Keep the reason in the same words if it appears in more than one place. The service card, the calendar day, and the error if they somehow submit anyway should not invent three explanations. One policy, one sentence.

Do not lecture. "This slot is for members" is complete. A paragraph about community is not going to land while they are late for something else. Firm and short fits the context. Charm can live on the confirmation, after they have what they came for.

If a time is held by someone mid-checkout, decide what the other guest sees. Taken, for a moment, is clearer than Open followed by a failure. If your hold is brief, you can say Limited while it is held, if that word matches the behavior. Do not say Open for a time you might reject.


Staff-only blocks are a common leak. A calendar that shows an internal meeting as a public hole, with no word, looks broken. If the guest should not know the block exists, show the surrounding open times and do not render a gap that implies a defect. If they should know the day is partly closed, say so on that day, in words. Gaps without words are the hidden-button problem in the shape of a calendar.

Reschedule rights belong on the confirmation the guest already trusts. If they can move the time and cannot change the service, say that next to the two controls. A single Edit that sometimes works and sometimes returns an error is the form of this bug they will screenshot. Split the verbs so the refusal is visible before the tap.
## Review it as a guest who expected a button

List the actions a guest will look for. Book a public service. Book a members-only service. Tap a taken time. Reschedule inside the window. Reschedule after the window. Deny calendar access and finish anyway.

For each one, mark hide, disable with a sentence, or explain with no button. Build those sentences. Then run the list on a phone in a private window, with a thumb, outdoors if you can. If you cannot read the reason at arm's length, the type is too small for the context. This guest is not at a desk.

When the calendar still does not show the service they were told about, they will search. The next piece is [search inside a booking product](/blog/search-inside-a-booking-product). Results have to be things they can book, in their words, with the same honesty about what is unavailable.

If you want the rules visible in the product instead of explained after a failed booking, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). A permission that shows up as a surprise error is a support script you will write anyway. Write it in the interface first.
